Extraction: Large Language Models for Security Operations Centers: A Comprehensive Survey (title page, p. 1). Review article (open access), presented by the authors as "the first comprehensive and structured analysis of LLM integration into SOC operations" (Abstract, p. 1).

Ali Habibzadeh, Farid Feyzi (corresponding author) and Reza Ebrahimi Atani, all with the Faculty of Engineering, University of Guilan, Rasht, Guilan, Iran (p. 1) — an academic-authored secondary study with no industry affiliation and no funding received (Funding statement, p. 28).

2026, Journal of Electrical and Computer Engineering (Wiley, open access), vol. 2026, article ID 3383674, DOI 10.1155/jece/3383674; received 14 December 2025, revised 25 April 2026, accepted 18 May 2026 (p. 1). A preprint was previously published on arXiv (2509.10858) (Disclosure, p. 28). Venue stratum caveat: Qualis A3 (PDR-0007).

SOCs face escalating operational strain — alert fatigue, excessive false positives and a critical skills gap — leading to delayed detections and delayed incident response (Abstract, p. 1; §1, p. 1): the SANS 2025 SOC survey identifies lack of skilled staff as the primary operational challenge (§1, p. 1), the Ponemon Institute reports an average of 258 days to identify and contain a breach (§1, p. 1), and Tier-1 analyst burnout and turnover increase the mean time to resolution for critical events (§2.2, p. 3). At the same time, the literature on LLMs in cybersecurity is fragmented: prior surveys are either too broad (security/privacy), too narrow (single tasks such as vulnerability detection), or pre-LLM SOC studies published before 2021, leaving no structured, operationally focused analysis of LLM integration across the distinct phases of SOC workflows (§2.4, p. 4; Table 2, p. 6).

A SECONDARY STUDY — no new system is built. The survey contributes (i) a foundational overview of SOC operations, analyst Tiers 1-4 and challenges (§2.2, pp. 3-4; Figure 2, p. 4); (ii) a dual-framework structured analysis mapping LLM applications across the SOC Detection/Analysis/Response phases to the NIST CSF functions, with MITRE ATT&CK as a granular lens for detection capabilities (§2.3, p. 4; Table 1, p. 5); and (iii) a research roadmap (§8, pp. 25-28). Agentic AI appears as one of five adaptation methods (pretraining, fine-tuning, prompt engineering, RAG, agents — §2.1, pp. 2-3) and is the dominant pattern in the Response phase: LLM-based agents/multi-agent systems are highly adopted in incident response (Table 14, p. 25), e.g., Audit-LLM's multiagent debate for insider-threat detection (§5.1, p. 8), IDS-Agent (Table 4, p. 10), RCACopilot deployed at Microsoft, RCAgent and Flow-of-Action for root cause analysis (§6.5, pp. 20-21; Table 12, p. 22), and Nissist, AutoBnB and IRCopilot for incident mitigation/response (§7.2, pp. 24-25). Maturity per task is assessed with a consolidated 4-stage TRL scale (§3.1, pp. 5-6).

Systematic literature review explicitly following Kitchenham's SLR guidelines (planning, conducting, reporting) (§3, p. 4). Five research questions (RQ1 LLMs used; RQ2-RQ4 adaptation per SOC phase; RQ5 challenges/future directions) (§3.1, p. 5). Search in five databases — ScienceDirect, SpringerLink, IEEE Xplore, ACM Digital Library, arXiv — supplemented by Google Scholar, with a declared Boolean search string combining LLM terms and SOC/cybersecurity terms (§3.2, p. 6). Inclusion: papers 2021-2025 that directly employ LLMs in their architecture with a SOC-aligned downstream task; exclusion: duplicates, non-English, non-full-length papers (books, short papers, tutorials); screening by title/abstract/conclusion with full-text review when ambiguous (§3.3, p. 6). Final corpus: 216 studies, whose per-year/per-phase distribution shows a sharp increase and a clear decline in volume from Detection to Response (§3.4, p. 6; Figure 3, p. 7). Maturity is assessed via the NASA/ISO 16290 TRL framework consolidated into four stages (§3.1, pp. 5-6). The paper reports no PRISMA flow diagram, no inter-rater reliability statistics and no formal quality appraisal of primary studies.

Secondary evidence only — the survey runs no empirical comparison of its own and reports no MTTD/MTTR measurements; all figures below are relayed from referenced primary studies. (1) Nissist [272] (LLM multi-agent incident mitigation at enterprise cloud scale): time-to-mitigate reduction of 98.93% for simple incidents and 94.85% for hard ones versus manual mitigation, with 77.19% / 52.63% full-automation success rates (§7.2, pp. 24-25). (2) AdaptiveLog [252]: ~73% average reduction in LLM-related costs across six log-analysis tasks — efficiency, not a time metric (§6.5, pp. 21-22). (3) Motivational context, not results: Ponemon's 258 days to identify and contain a breach (§1, p. 1) and burnout-driven increases in mean time to resolution (§2.2, p. 3). MTTR appears explicitly only as a recommended future measurement: SOC engineers should pilot agent-based RAG for alert enrichment and "measure the reduction in mean time to respond (MTTR)" before broadening deployment (§8.2, p. 27). No MTTD figures appear anywhere in the paper.

Field: General Impact on Agentic AI / Multi-Agent Systems
Extraction: The survey positions agents as the architectural answer to the hardest SOC tasks while flagging their cost: agent-based systems incur higher computational overhead from iterative reasoning, multiple model calls and tool interactions (§2.1, p. 3). For root cause analysis, LLM-based agents are deemed the more suitable choice because they can interact with external environments, synthesize high-volume multisource data, adapt without retraining and explain their outputs (§6.5, p. 20). In incident response, multiagent architectures mimic human IR team structures with specialized collaborative components, mitigating factual inaccuracy and context loss common in monolithic LLMs, and are called "a transformative approach for more efficient and effective IR" (§7.2, p. 25; Table 14, p. 25). Named agentic exemplars include Audit-LLM (pairwise evidence-based multiagent debate, §5.1, p. 8), RCAgent with observation-snapshot-key context compression validated on Alibaba Cloud (§6.5, p. 21) and AutoBnB simulating IR team structures (§7.2, p. 24; Table 14, p. 25). Future directions push the field toward agent-based RAG, autonomous security decision-making under human supervision, and formal human-in-the-loop (HITL) protocols with escalation paths and override-feedback registries (§8.2, pp. 26-27); the reference list includes dedicated Agentic AI literature (refs. [289-290], p. 38).

Challenges catalogued for LLMs in SOCs (§8.1, pp. 25-26): resource intensity and financial barriers; hallucination and bias (fabricated threat indicators, false-positive escalations); black-box opacity and catastrophic forgetting; attack-surface expansion (prompt injection, data poisoning, model inversion); a data trilemma (availability, relevance/concept drift, text-vs-nonlinguistic structure mismatch); integration with heterogeneous SOC stacks lacking standardized APIs; regulatory compliance (GDPR/HIPAA vs. opaque commercial APIs); and balancing human expertise with automation. Research gaps: coverage is heavily concentrated on NIST "Detect", with significant gaps in "Protect" and especially "Recover" (Table 1, p. 5; §8.2, pp. 27-28; §9, p. 28), and the Response phase is the least researched due to operational risk, scarce real-world datasets and missing IR benchmarks (§3.4, p. 6; §7.2, p. 25). Future directions (§8.2, pp. 26-28): XAI for SOC trust, LLM+federated learning, robust benchmarks and SOC simulation environments, agent-based RAG, autonomous decision-making with phased low-risk rollout, hybrid rule-based/ML/LLM architectures, HITL protocols, and filling the Protect/Recover gaps. As a survey, it also carries methodological limitations it does not discuss: no quality appraisal, no inter-rater statistics and no PRISMA reporting (§3, pp. 4-6).

Directly relevant as domain-mapping foundation: it is the first structured survey of exactly the environment where my proposed agentic copilot operates (LLMs across SOC detection, analysis and incident response), and it independently corroborates the thesis problem framing — skills gap, alert fatigue and delayed response quantified via SANS 2025 and Ponemon's 258-day containment window (§1, p. 1). It supplies reusable scaffolding (NIST CSF x MITRE ATT&CK mapping, Table 1, p. 5; 4-stage TRL maturity, §3.1, pp. 5-6), a catalogue of agentic IR systems to position the copilot against (Nissist, AutoBnB, IRCopilot — Table 14, p. 25), secondary MTTR-adjacent evidence (Nissist's 94.85-98.93% time-to-mitigate reduction, §7.2, pp. 24-25), and an explicit research-gap argument the thesis exploits: Response is the least-studied phase and agent-based RAG pilots should be evaluated by MTTR reduction (§8.2, p. 27). Corpus status: enters as a foundational-conditional SECONDARY study under rule R1 — usable for background, taxonomy and gap justification, not as primary MTTD/MTTR evidence — with the mandatory stratum caveat: venue is Qualis A3 (PDR-0007).

Medium — High thematic overlap (LLM/agentic systems for SOC incident response, with explicit MTTR framing and a Response-phase gap the thesis addresses), but it is a secondary study with no primary MTTD/MTTR evidence of its own, published in a Qualis A3 venue, so it serves as foundational context and gap justification rather than core empirical evidence (R1; PDR-0007).
